articles.title: 'A particular issue': Penguin India on impasse over Sonia Gandhi memoir
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Penguin Random House India on Monday said publication of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir in India had stalled after the publisher and the author’s re.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Penguin Random House India on Monday said publication of Sonia Gandhi’s memoir in India had stalled after the publisher and the author’s representatives reached an “impasse over a particular issue.” The publisher also firmly denied that any external pressure had influenced the decision.Penguin India said the disagreement emerged during its normal editorial review of Belonging: A Journey of Love, which it had been keen to publish.The clarification came amid a growing political controversy over the memoir’s India publication, after Alfred A Knopf, the US-based imprint of Penguin Random House, announced that the book would be released worldwide on November 10. While Congress leaders have raised questions about possible governmental pressure and freedom of expression, Penguin India said the disagreement was strictly part of the editorial process.“On some, they agreed to changes and on others, we accepted the author’s position. Unfortunately, and ultimately, an understanding could not be reached on a particular issue,” the publisher said.PRHI spokesperson Pallavi Narayan said the publishing house had been “really keen” to bring out the memoir, describing it as “a hard-won acquisition”.“We feel it is important for us to correct certain misrepresentations regarding the forthcoming memoir 'Belonging'. This is a book that we at Penguin Random House India, were really keen on publishing as it was a hard-won acquisition,” Narayan said in an exclusive statement to PTI.The publisher said the manuscript had gone through its “normal editorial process”, during which several points were raised and discussed with the author’s representatives. Some proposed changes were accepted, while on other matters Penguin India accepted the author’s position.It was ultimately the unresolved issue that brought the publication process to a halt, according to PRHI. The author’s team subsequently informed the publisher that they did not wish to proceed with the publication, a decision the publishing house said it respected.At the same time, Penguin India rejected suggestions that the impasse was the result of intervention from outside the publishing process.“Since the content of the book is confidential and under embargo, there was no external pressure whatsoever,” the publisher said.PRHI declined to reveal the nature of the disputed issue, citing its contractual obligations and commitment to author confidentiality.“Since we are bound by an agreement, and author confidentiality is paramount to us, we will not divulge details of what led to the impasse,” the publisher said.The publishing house also defended its decision to scrutinise the manuscript, saying editorial assessment, questioning, fact-checking and recommendations were part of its responsibility as a publisher.“As publishers, it was its “responsibility and duty” to critically assess a manuscript, ask questions, make recommendations and exercise its independent editorial judgement,” Penguin India said.The controversy intensified after reports that Penguin India had backed out of publishing the memoir following disagreements over editorial changes. Former Rajasthan chief minister Ashok Gehlot alleged that pressure had been put on Penguin India to remove sections concerning Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the RSS and China’s occupation of Indian territory during the Modi government.Former Madhya Pradesh chief minister Kamal Nath also questioned whether the publisher’s position had been influenced by pressure from elsewhere.Penguin India’s latest statement, however, maintains that no such external intervention took place and that the disagreement arose solely during the editorial process.The memoir is expected to offer a rare account of Gandhi’s life, covering her childhood in post-war Italy, her marriage into the Nehru-Gandhi family, the assassination of her husband and former prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, and her subsequent entry into politics.While the international edition is scheduled for release on November 10, the status of its publication in India remains unresolved.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.body:
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Smoke from forest and peatland fires burning across Indonesia has pushed air quality in parts of Malaysian Borneo to hazardous levels, triggering a surge in respiratory illness and forcing the cancellation of outdoor Independence Day celebrations.

The smoke – drifting from fires in Kalimantan in the Indonesian portion of the island of Borneo – has settled over the Malaysian state of Sarawak, on the same island, for much of August. It has also reached peninsular Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore.

It is the region’s worst haze episode since 2015, when fires in Indonesia exposed tens of millions of people to toxic smoke and caused more than 500,000 people to suffer respiratory ailments.

On Tuesday, six areas in Sarawak recorded hazardous air quality, with readings above 300 on Malaysia’s Air Pollutant Index. Anything above 100 is considered unhealthy. In Kuching, the state capital, the index hit 407, while in Serian, a town close to the Kalimantan border, it hit 408.

Mia Emylia Hassan, 33, a mother of two in Kuching, said the smell of smoke was inescapable.

“The air here is very thick,” she said. “It smells like smoke, and it’s just white all over.” Visibility from her house, she said, had dropped to about a kilometre, or roughly half a mile. “We have not seen blue sky for over a month,” she said.

The haze arrived in early August, shortly after her 10-month-old daughter came home from the hospital after a lung infection. “She’s not healing properly because her lungs are still developing,” Hassan said. “She’s been on medication this whole month, and she has been coughing and vomiting.”

Twice, the family has had to rush the infant back to the emergency room because she could not breathe.

“It’s a mini heart attack for us every time,” Hassan said.

Malaysia’s Ministry of Health has reported a sharp rise in illness nationwide. During the week of August 23 to 29, asthma cases climbed to 1,811, up from 219 the previous week, the ministry said on Saturday, while conjunctivitis cases also rose to 720, from 146.

In peninsular Malaysia, Karen-Michaela Tan, an asthma patient who lives near the capital, Kuala Lumpur, said that a week after the haze thickened, she was “wheezing audibly” and “breathless when climbing stairs”. The 52-year-old said she needed two nebuliser treatments back to back to stop the wheezing, along with a heavy dose of steroids.

“Doctors are erring on the side of caution when it comes to asthma patients, choosing to up dosages rather than risk a patient being hospitalised for shortness of breath,” she said.

Her house is sealed, and two purifiers run continuously. Still, “I battle throat scratchiness and nasal dryness even with these measures”, she said.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), a regional bloc, has activated a Level 3 transboundary haze alert – its highest – for the southern part of the region. The alert signals a high risk of severe cross-border haze. ASEAN cited an increase in fire hotspots and prolonged dry weather, fuelled by an intensifying El Nino weather pattern.

The toxic smoke has forced Sarawak to cancel its outdoor Independence Day celebrations on Monday, and officials warned that worse restrictions could follow. Any area where readings cross 500 will be placed under a local emergency, and all public and private offices will be closed, the deputy premier, Douglas Uggah Embas, told reporters. “Only essential services will be allowed to operate,” he added.

In Kuala Lumpur, where skies were grey for most of the month, the haze thinned enough to reveal blue sky for the first time in a week, just as the Independence Day parade got under way early in the morning.

Schools, too, have been hit hard. Under Ministry of Education rules, outdoor activities are suspended when the index reaches 100, and schools must close at 200. On August 20 and 21, nearly 600 schools in and around Kuching shut, affecting some 200,000 primary and secondary students. And on August 28, 30 more schools in Sarawak closed, keeping more than 4,000 children at home.

This week, schools are closed for the Independence Day holiday.

Youth sport has been affected, too. Yap Kai Jinn, 31, a coach at Square One Football, a Kuala Lumpur academy, said the club had cancelled all training sessions and matches since last week.

“Along with our parents, we decided that it is not healthy; it is not safe for our players to play under these conditions,” he said. “For now, we are looking for an enclosed area to do sessions, and for outdoor, we have to wait and hope that the weather gets better.”

The toll of the haze has been far heavier in Indonesia.

The country’s deputy health minister, Dante Saksono Harbuwono, told reporters on Monday that some 13,500 people were treated for respiratory infections in July and August, while about 5.5 million people on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra have been directly exposed to smoke.

Borneo is the world’s third-largest island and is divided between Indonesia, which controls the southern two-thirds as Kalimantan; Malaysia, whose states of Sarawak and Sabah run along the north; as well as the sultanate of Brunei.

According to the Indonesian government, fires between January and July burned more than 200,000 hectares (about 494,000 acres), an area three times the size of Indonesia’s capital, Jakarta, across Borneo and Sumatra. Nearly 95,000 hectares (about 235,000 acres) burned in July alone.

And despite efforts to control the blazes, the fires continue to surge in parts of Indonesian Borneo.

Hotspots in West Kalimantan nearly doubled on Monday, rising by 3,553 to 7,377, while the number of active fires rose by 88 to 104, and visibility fell below a kilometre, said Berton Panjaitan, an official at Indonesia’s National Disaster Mitigation Agency. In Central Kalimantan, hotspots declined by 147 to 5,244, while fire spots increased by 16 to 72, he said.

Cities in Kalimantan have recorded hazardous air, too.

Readings in Palangkaraya in Central Kalimantan reached 780 on Monday on the air quality index used by IQAir, a Swiss company that monitors pollution data. Pontianak in West Kalimantan reached 593.

The fires are largely set on purpose, analysts say, with plantation companies and smallholders alike burning rainforest and carbon-rich peatland to clear ground for palm oil, farming, and pulp and paper production. The practice is illegal, and Indonesian police said last week that they had arrested 72 people suspected of setting recent fires.

Researchers warned people in Southeast Asia to brace for a long fire season.

El Nino – the naturally occurring pattern that shifts winds, air pressure and rainfall worldwide – appears headed for “super” strength, said Helena Varkkey, a specialist on transboundary haze at Universiti Malaya.

In Southeast Asia, she said, “the intensifying El Nino means hotter and drier conditions”, so “any fires that happen will have a bigger and longer regional impact”.

Jayaprakash Muralitharan, a Malaysian atmospheric scientist, said the worst was still ahead.

Haze conditions are “going to be severe and longer, because the hot weather started much earlier last year”, he said. “El Nino came in and made conditions drier. Now you have the extreme drying of the peatland.”

And peat can make fires stubborn, he said. What looks extinguished on the surface can smoulder underground for weeks and flare up again, and nothing short of sustained rain will soak the soil enough to put it out.

Until the rains arrive, Muralitharan said, there is little to be done.

“Human intervention now is only a temporary solution. It would go on until end of September or October when the rain comes in. I hope that rain comes in by then.”

images.caption: Tourists look at the city skyline, shrouded in haze from wildfires in Indonesia, in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on August 12, 2026 [Hasnoor Hussain/ Reuters]

articles.title: CBS News takes heat over report on Dem hopeful Abdul El-Sayed's now-deleted 9/11 posts
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's deleted 9/11 social media posts sparked a firestorm after CBS News reported on the Michigan Senate candidate's past comments.
articles.body: CBS News faced heat from the far-left Monday over a report about past comments Democratic Michigan Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed made about 9/11 ahead of the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack. "As the nation prepares to mark 25 years since Sept. 11, 2001, Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, may be facing the risk of renewed scrutiny and fresh political attack," CBS News wrote Monday. The report cited El-Sayed's deleted social media posts, including some from 2020 comparing the nearly 3,000 Americans killed on 9/11 to the death toll from the coronavirus pandemic. Another post from Sept. 11, 2021, first uncovered by The Washington Free Beacon, read, "Today, I mourn the 3K lives, 6K injuries, & infrastructural devastation in NYC, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my faith. Tomorrow, I'll mourn ~1M lives, millions of injuries, & infrastructural devastation in 3 countries, perpetuated ignorantly in the name of my country." UNEARTHED EL-SAYED ESSAY DRAWS EXPLOSIVE TRUMP-BIN LADEN PARALLEL: ‘RECRUITED, RADICALIZED AND REASSURED’ However, many of El-Sayed's supporters and other liberal critics expressed outrage linking El-Sayed to the forthcoming 9/11 anniversary. "What an insane headline," far-left commentator Hasan Piker reacted on X. "This is why the [new Paramount owner David Ellison] bought CBS and put Bari Weiss in charge." Bari Weiss was tapped by Ellison to become the network's editor-in-chief last fall as part of Paramount's multimillion-dollar acquisition of her outlet The Free Press. "Hi @CBS @CBSNews @bariweiss do you think it's super offensive and disgusting and Islamophobic to do a tweet about the potential first ever Muslim Democratic senator which begins by referencing 9/11?" Zeteo founder and former MSNBC host Mehdi Hasan asked. "Despicable anti-Muslim woke right garbage from the house CBS account," The Bulwark podcast host and MS NOW analyst Tim Miller wrote. SOCIALIST CANDIDATES CAN DELETE OLD POSTS, BUT THEY CAN'T ERASE THEIR RADICALISM "What an insane, blatantly racist headline. Unreal," Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., posted. "The current state of institutional media legit bums me out," Vox host and editorial director Astead Herndon said. "We’ve burned through so much credibility in recent years. And our information ecosystem is worse for it." YOUTUBE STAR MS RACHEL GIVES FUNDS TO DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED A CBS News source familiar with the story shrugged off the criticism, telling Fox News Digital that reports about deleted social media posts from politicians are published "all the time." El-Sayed was confronted about his deleted posts by a local CBS News reporter on the campaign trail. "What happened on 9/11 is a disaster. It was a terrible attack on our country," El-Sayed said. "And our responsibility is also to think about, how do we build an America where we are protecting our servicemen and women from being asked to fight in wars we have no business fighting in?" CBS News did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

articles.title: Duane "Keffe D" Davis found guilty in 1996 murder of rapper Tupac Shakur
articles.summary: The verdict ends decades of mystery as to who was behind the rapper's death.
articles.body:
Former gang boss Duane "Keffe D" Davis has been found guilty of orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur - the first conviction in a cold case that has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

The jury found Davis guilty of one count of murder with a deadly weapon for the rap superstar's death in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996.

Clad in a black suit, the 63-year-old stood impassively in the Las Vegas court as the verdict was read, before saying he would appeal. Shakur's relatives held hands, some hugging and crying.

Shakur was 25 when he was slain at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.

Tupac murder accused told police in 2008 his nephew fired fatal shots

What to know about Tupac's murder trial and the gang leader accused of orchestrating his death

Prosecutors had argued during the trial that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not fire the gun that killed Shakur, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.

They told the court that Davis had planned the shooting as retaliation after Anderson was involved in a fight with Shakur and the rapper's crew in Las Vegas just hours earlier.

For 30 years, the case remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - but never a conviction, until now.

Shakur's murder happened at a time of intense rivalry between the East Coast and West Coast rap scene and amid gang feuds between the Bloods and Crips, which had deep roots within hip-hop at the time.

His family appeared emotional in court, his sister embracing a prosecutor after the verdict was read while others sat crying nearby.

Outside, devoted fans of Shakur were crying and cheering.

The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, where he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.

He had told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview related to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace.

Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.

But his book and media interviews voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges being filed, with the court ruling his police interview could be used in the murder trial against him.

In closing arguments, prosecutor Binu Palal told jurors to take Davis at his word and find him guilty.

For years, he argued, Davis had been telling people "that he is responsible for Tupac Shakur's murder" through documentaries, his memoir, podcasts and a police interview.

"He's the shot caller - in every instance in every iteration he's the leader of the South Side Crips," Palal told the jury.

"When you have the shot caller sitting shotgun when shots are fired, there's no doubt he's responsible."

Tupac murder trial: 'All hell broke loose' night of rapper's shooting, witness says

Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.

In closing arguments, his lawyer Michael Sanft urged the jury to discredit his client as a liar who just told tales to sell books.

But within hours of the jury being handed the case on Monday, they reached a guilty verdict.

Just before the court emptied out, Clark County District Court Judge Carli Kierny set Davis' sentencing for 13 October.

While reading out some procedural steps in the case, Davis appeared to interrupt by raising his hand.

"I would like my stuff," he told the judge, mentioning some personal items including his phone.

He continued: "I would like to appeal this matter."

The judge explained that this could happen after sentencing.

Get all the latest trial updates on the BBC Sounds ' Fame Under Fire: The Tupac Murder Trial ' podcast available wherever you get your BBC podcasts.

articles.title: US brings back Russia’s Siluanov to G20 finance talks, angering Europe
articles.summary: Anton Siluanov holds talks with US counterpart as European officials object to Russia’s return to G20 talks.
articles.body:
Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov has made a surprise appearance at United States-hosted G20 finance talks in North Carolina, sparking frustration and dismay among European ministers and officials.

Siluanov’s appearance at the talks in Asheville on Monday marks the first time the minister, who was appointed in 2011, has attended a G20 meeting in person since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, with Russia’s Ministry of Finance saying the two men discussed financial cooperation within the G20 framework.

A US official said the meeting focused on US President Donald Trump’s peace plan for Ukraine.

Asked about the invitation to Siluanov, Trump told reporters: “We like getting along with everybody. One of the reasons I’m so successful, I get along with everybody.”

European officials, however, criticised the move.

Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski said he was unhappy to see Moscow represented, although he recognised the right of G20 hosts to invite guests.

“We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly, and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them,” ⁠he told the Reuters news agency, stressing that Russia was the aggressor in its conflict with Ukraine.

“So for me, it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia.”

German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said the US’s decision to welcome Siluanov sent a “signal I find troubling”.

He said he told Siluanov during a plenary session that Moscow had to end the war and “that we clearly support Ukraine”.

He also said Europe was preparing a further package of sanctions against Russia and hoped for close cooperation with Washington on the measures.

European ministers and central bankers also opposed appearing with Siluanov in the traditional G20 “family photo”, European officials said. The photograph was ultimately taken without the Russian minister.

Klingbeil said European officials, including European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, had discussed Russia’s involvement on Sunday and agreed that maintaining an avenue for dialogue could allow them to deliver a frank message to Moscow.

“However, the mere fact that the Russian finance minister is back – after, I believe, four G20 meetings without Russian participation – indicates an attempt at normalisation, and that makes it all the more important for us to push back,” he said.

Siluanov’s appearance marked a sharp contrast with the G20 meeting in Washington, DC, in April 2022, when his virtual participation prompted officials from Canada, the United Kingdom, the US, and the European Central Bank to walk out.

Asked about Siluanov’s attendance, White House spokesman Kush Desai told the AFP news agency that the Trump administration had been working with Russia to push for a deal that “would stop the endless bloodshed that the president has really condemned”.

“The president and the administration will never shy away from talking with the folks we need to talk to, to further that,” he said. “That’s what we’re working on here at the G20.”

Separately, Reuters and AFP, citing sources familiar with the Washington-Moscow talks, said Bessent had made clear that the US would not provide Russia with economic relief until war in Ukraine was over.

Trump has pushed Moscow and Kyiv to reach a deal to halt the fighting, but an initial 28-point plan that largely adhered to Russia’s demands was criticised by Ukraine and European governments.

The US, which currently holds the rotating G20 presidency, did not invite South Africa, last year’s G20 host, to the gathering. Poland, which is not a permanent G20 member, was invited.

Certain reporters from major US newsrooms, including The New York Times and Bloomberg News, were not granted credentials to cover the gathering.

The decision was condemned by the National Press Club, which said that “no administration should be allowed to handpick the press corps that scrutinizes it”.

The two-day meeting comes as global debt levels have reached a record of nearly $353 trillion and the global economy faces an energy shock triggered by the US-Israel war on Iran. The talks also come amid rising tensions over China’s large trade surplus and uncertainty over the effects of a surge in artificial intelligence investment.

images.caption: Russia's Finance Minister Anton Siluanov attends a plenary session as finance ministers and central bank governors from G20 countries meet in Asheville, North Carolina, US, August 31, 2026 [Sam Wolfe/Reuters]

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, CEO of JPMorgan Chase Jamie Dimon and CEO of Goldman Sachs David M Solomon attend a plenary session as finance ministers and central bank governors from G20 countries meet in Asheville [Sam Wolfe/Reuters]

articles.title: Andy Burnham to face Parliament as prime minister for first time
articles.summary: This may well be the point when his honeymoon period as PM ends and the hard work begins, Damian Grammaticas writes.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham is set to speak in the Commons later, addressing MPs on their first day back at work after the summer recess, in what will be a highly charged moment.

Six weeks after he walked up Downing Street, and 16 years after he last appeared at the dispatch box as part of a Labour government, he will stand before MPs for the first time as prime minister.

In the close confines of the chamber, with ranks of Labour members behind him, Burnham will finally come face to face with his political opponents.

The pressure of the occasion, the scrutiny he will face, the deftness with which he handles questions, the attacks, the barbs, the asides, will all be key to how the public perceive him.

Burnham's summer tour is over - now he has to prove himself in Parliament

Burnham gets the early prison release changes he wanted - but at what cost?

Mel Stride and Priti Patel replaced in major Tory reshuffle

Sports Direct founder attacks Burnham's 'populist' High Street plans

Burnham says he will not vote on assisted dying unlike Starmer

Downing Street does not want to give too much away but we know he will meet his cabinet before delivering a statement "setting out the direction of his government" and facing questions from MPs.

A Number 10 source said over the weekend that Burnham did not want his government to "stand by and watch on as every bill goes up and up".

So he "will promise the country that wherever we can make life more affordable we will".

Burnham has had a relatively easy summer. When he became prime minister, MPs were already on their break.

So he has been free to travel the country unveiling policies designed to help with the cost of living: a £2 cap on bus fares; removing VAT from domestic energy bills; and cutting business rates for pubs, clubs and music venues by 20% next year.

But now the challenges he will face having ousted Sir Keir Starmer begin. And there is an autumn packed with political tests coming.

There will be his first session of Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, then the spotlight of the party conferences, his first Budget and, later in the year, a speech where he will lay out a 10-year plan for the country.

It is thought this week he may say more about his plans to bring privatised services back under public control, arguing that doing so will help ease the pressure on family budgets.

Number 10 says Burnham will tell MPs he will keep taking action on the cost of living.

The Conservatives and Reform UK, however, are preparing to attack his policies, questioning how they will be funded and whether there will be new tax rises.

Kemi Badenoch reshuffled her shadow cabinet team on Monday in preparation for this moment. To sharpen her party's attacks on Labour over its handling of tax and the economy she promoted Andrew Griffith to be her new shadow chancellor.

The Conservatives are making much of his past jobs in business. Before entering politics he was chief financial officer and chief operating officer at Sky, and chair of Just Eat.

He is promising a Conservative government that would deliver "lower, simpler taxes, get Britain drilling again to bring down energy costs, slash the red tape holding Britain back, and scrap the job-killing measures in Labour's (Un)Employment Rights Act".

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have seized on the fact Griffith was a Treasury minister in Liz Truss's government and publicly defended her "mini-budget".

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour Party chair, said the "Tories' top team is crammed full of the same vandals who hammered family finances and left our public services crumbling".

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said Griffith's appointment showed the Conservatives were "happy to forfeit any claim to economic credibility".

Burnham will face criticism from the Greens too. Their leader, Zack Polanski, says that Burnham's ideas for greater public control over vital services is "just tinkering".

Polanski says "if he really wants to bring back hope, he needs to tax the wealthy, take water and energy back under public ownership, bring in rent controls, and say no to new North Sea drilling".

The Liberal Democrats are already attacking Burnham's plans to deal with the prisons crisis.

Their justice spokesperson, Jess Brown-Fuller, said Labour's promise to build new cells was not backed by any new money and proved "just how unserious this Government remains about fixing our justice system".

Other major challenges facing Burnham include defence. How will he fund the plans he has inherited from Sir Keir? And, beyond that, how fast will he increase spending to meet Nato commitments?

There are imminent decisions to be made about whether to approve new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea. There are looming choices about whether to do more to help as energy bills rise this winter, whether to increase taxes at the Budget. And longer-term issues about reforms to welfare, social care and ties with the EU.

All of which means that the moment when Burnham rises to address MPs on Tuesday may well be the point when his honeymoon period as prime minister ends and the hard work begins.

articles.title: 100-year-old Hindu temple demolished in Pakistan’s Punjab
articles.summary: Pakistan News: A more than 100-year-old Hindu temple in Pakistan’s Punjab province was demolished on August 21 in Siraj village of Narowal, around 130 km from Lahore.
articles.body: A more than 100-year-old Hindu temple in Pakistan’s Punjab province was demolished on August 21 in Siraj village of Narowal, around 130 km from Lahore, with minority groups alleging that religious zealots targeted the site to absorb its land into an adjacent madrassa. The government, however, has maintained that the temple collapsed because of torrential rains.The demolition has triggered demands for an investigation and restoration of the temple, with the Pakistan Masiha Millat Party (PMMP) accusing local authorities and the Evacuee Trust Property Board (ETPB) of failing to protect the centuries-old Hindu place of worship.PMMP chairman Aslam Parvez Sahotra said he met Punjab Additional Home Secretary on August 28 and submitted a written application seeking action against those allegedly responsible for the demolition, as well as officials accused of failing to protect the property.Sahotra alleged that the people involved in the demolition were associated with the Tehreek-i-Labbaik Pakistan (TLP), a banned far-right Islamic party. He further claimed that after the temple was brought down, metal fittings from its shikhar, bricks and other material were removed from the site.The temple, estimated to be between 100 and 125 years old, stood on approximately 1,000 square metres of land in Siraj village.The dispute over the site predates its demolition. According to Sahotra, land adjoining the temple had earlier been leased by the ETPB for a madrassa. The lease was subsequently cancelled after rent allegedly went unpaid for several years and the premises were not used for the stated purpose.He said several people later occupied portions of the property illegally.Sahotra referred to a revenue department report which identified individuals as illegal occupants of the temple’s quarters and other parts of the property. He said the ETPB deputy administrator in Sialkot cancelled the seminary’s lease rights on January 29, 2026, and ordered the eviction of illegal occupants and sealing of the property.“This order was not implemented,” Sahotra alleged.A report attributed to the DSP Narowal, dated April 11, also indicated that local police were aware of security concerns surrounding the temple and the possibility that it could be damaged, according to Sahotra.The ETPB, however, has rejected the allegation that the temple was deliberately demolished.ETPB senior official Rana Iftikhar told PTI that the temple had collapsed following torrential rains. He acknowledged its historical significance, saying, “The temple carries no name in our record books. However, it is a very old one... more than 100 to 125 years old,” he said.Iftikhar also confirmed that the land adjoining the temple had been leased for a seminary, but maintained that the temple's own land had not been leased.“However, the temple's land is not given to anyone for lease,” he said and added the ETPB highups will decide about restoration of the temple.The conflicting accounts have heightened concerns among members of the local Hindu community.Hindu community leader Rattan Lal condemned the demolition and called for the government to order the temple's restoration. He said the district administration and ETPB had failed to take adequate steps to secure the site or remove alleged illegal occupants.“The district administration and the ETPB failed to take adequate measures to protect the site or remove the alleged occupants, ultimately allowing the temple to be demolished,” Lal said and asked the government to take action against those found involved in the demolition of the temple.Lal, who is also a Hindu member of the Narowal District Peace Committee and the Pak Dharam Astan Hindu Committee, said members of the community were now reluctant to approach the site.“We are even afraid to visit the site because of the madrassa that continues to operate on its premises.”Sahotra has called for the temple to be rebuilt in its original form and urged the Punjab government to strengthen protection for Hindu temples, Sikh gurdwaras and Christian churches, along with their adjoining properties.Arya, meanwhile, said decades of conflict between Pakistan and India, the Islamisation policies of the 1980s and the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid in India had contributed to a sense of insecurity among local Hindus.“Preserving Hindu heritage can improve the image of Pakistan and attract tourism.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Fast-acting principal in Nepal evacuated 900 students before flooding swept away their school
articles.summary: Rajendra Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage in the aftermath of flash floods that killed almost 1,000 people and left thousands of others missing.
articles.body: BIDUR, Nepal — Rajendra Dawadi was inside his classroom when a colleague rushed in with a warning: Floodwaters were racing through Nepal’s Trishuli Valley, tearing apart homes, bridges and entire villages. Then a teacher received another warning by phone. Moments later, a parent arrived to take her child home. The danger had not yet been confirmed, but Dawadi, the principal, had little time to act. He rang the school bell and ordered his students and staff out of the building and toward higher ground. “I immediately decided to stop ... school” and get the children out, he told The Associated Press. As he followed them to a nearby hill, the floodwaters rose behind him. From the safety of the hillside, he turned to watch the school where he had once been a student — and where he had spent years teaching — disappear beneath a torrent of water, mud, boulders and debris. Two staff members could not make it and remain missing. Dawadi’s decision to evacuate the school saved at least 900 students from last week’s devastating flash floods in Nepal, unleashed after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas. The disaster killed over 950 people in Nepal and Tibet, while more than 4,400 remain missing. As Nepal grapples with the catastrophic natural disaster, Dawadi’s story has emerged as a striking example of foresight and courage. The Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School had 1,643 students. At least 900 were on campus that morning, while some students were still making their way to school. Dawadi ordered those already there to leave and called bus drivers to tell them not to come. One bus, packed with students, had already reached the school when Dawadi told the driver to turn back, he said. The bus crossed a newly constructed bridge and, moments later, the old bridge beside it collapsed. For Dawadi, the scale of the destruction has become personal, as the school had been both his workplace and a large part of his life. “I have no words. I got education from that school. And I gave education at that school,” he said. The destruction of Dawadi’s school was not an isolated loss. Across northern Nepal, the floods have left thousands of children without classrooms, disrupted their education and raised fears that the disaster could cost them months of schooling. Aid group Save the Children said in a statement that at least 69 schools in northern Nepal were destroyed, putting the education of nearly 19,000 students at risk. Dawadi’s quick thinking and swift response during the disaster have been hailed as an act of heroism. When he returned to the site of the school days later, parents embraced him as they thanked him for saving their children. “Their parents hugged me, they cried with me,” he said. “They were emotional.” Student Suvina Tamang, 14, said the building was swept away shortly after the students had been evacuated. “I will thank him when I see him” for saving my life, she said. But Dawadi is reluctant to accept the role of hero. For him, rescuing his students was his responsibility. Now, he says, students will need psychological counseling. Then, lessons must begin again, even if the school must temporarily relocate. His appeal to the Nepalese government is simple: Rebuild the schools and get children back to classes.

articles.title: Shares in fast fashion retailer Shein slide in long-delayed Hong Kong debut
articles.summary: The company has faced tariff and duty changes in the U.S. and Europe, along with intense scrutiny of its business practices that hampered its attempts to list in New York and London.
articles.body: HONG KONG — Shares in online fast-fashion retailer Shein fell 8% in their first day of Hong Kong trade on Tuesday, with investors worried about the impact of setbacks that long delayed its listing and have undermined its competitive advantages. Known globally for selling $5 tops and $10 dresses, Shein has been humbled by tariff and duty changes in the U.S. and Europe. Intense scrutiny of its business practices in the West also hampered its attempts to list in New York and London, which were ultimately blocked by Chinese authorities. The stock was trading at around 44.6 Hong Kong dollars ($5.68) in morning trade, valuing the company at around $24 billion ($3 billion), far below its 2022 peak of nearly $100 billion ($12.8 billion). Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index was down 0.6%. “As a new company listed in Hong Kong, we will continue to innovate, optimize and cooperate with our supply chain partners for mutual benefit and win-win results,” Shein Chief Financial Officer Leigh Gui said at the opening gong ceremony. Founder and CEO Sky Xu, known for disliking the limelight, did not speak at the event though later took pictures with Shein employees onstage. He declined to respond to Reuters’ questions. “I think the weak debut shows that even after the huge valuation reset, investors still don’t see Shein as obviously cheap,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. Chanana said Shein was valued at 15 times forward earnings, more than double the multiple for PDD, the owner of rival Temu, which meant “investors were being asked to pay a premium despite weaker growth visibility and significant regulatory and trade risks.” Demand for Shein’s stock during the IPO was tepid compared with high-profile offerings from the AI and robotics sectors. The retail tranche was subscribed 5.63 times, while the international portion was subscribed 2.59 ​times. Some deals have been hundreds of times oversubscribed, especially from Hong Kong’s army of retail investors who track IPOs very closely. The amount sold in the IPO represents about 6.6% of Shein’s enlarged share capital. Cornerstone investors took about one-fifth of the IPO and are locked up for six months, leaving roughly 5% freely tradable. Last year, the U.S. ended the de minimis duty exemption for e-commerce shipments under $800 that had powered Shein’s direct-shipping model. The European Union recently followed suit, imposing fees on low-value packages. Shein’s net income slid 39% last year, and it swung to a loss in the first quarter. Shein has said it expects first-half operating profit margin to be slightly lower than in the first quarter, hurt by higher customs duties, tariffs, fees and logistics costs in Europe and the Middle East. “New markets could help offset slower growth in the U.S. and Europe, but lower spending power in developing markets may limit the benefit if delivery costs stay high,” said Lorraine Tan, director of equity research at Morningstar. Shein has been trying to widen beyond its own-label ultra-cheap fast fashion, having expanded its third-party marketplace and bought U.S. apparel brand Everlane in May. In its prospectus, it said it aims to offer marketplace and supply chain services to more brands, in the footsteps of French brand Pimkie and British brand Missguided, which it bought in 2023. The IPO has helped Shein compensate early investors who invested at much higher valuations. The company has agreed to make cash payments totaling about $3.5 billion and share adjustments to some preferred shareholders. “This IPO is not just a fundraising event — it is also, and probably more of, a capital-structure event,” said Jianggan Li, CEO of consultancy Momentum Works.

articles.title: She sold fruits to fund her education, then became a cancer-care pioneer: The remarkable journey of Dr Vijayalakshmi Deshmane
articles.summary: Some of the most remarkable medical journeys begin far from hospitals and operating rooms. For Dr Vijayalakshmi Deshmane, the path to becoming a pione.
articles.body: Some of the most remarkable medical journeys begin far from hospitals and operating rooms. For Dr Vijayalakshmi Deshmane, the path to becoming a pioneering surgical oncologist began after school, helping her mother sell fruits and vegetables to support their struggling family. She faced financial hardship, a language barrier and even academic failure, moments that nearly forced her to abandon her dream of becoming a doctor. Yet she returned, persevered and eventually broke barriers in surgical oncology. From a modest childhood in Karnataka to becoming a respected cancer specialist and Padma Shri awardee, Deshmane’s life is a powerful story of resilience, courage and service.A childhood shaped by sacrificeBorn in 1955, Deshmane grew up in a financially struggling family. Her father, Baburao Deshmane, worked as a labourer and was also a freedom fighter, while her mother, Ratnamma, sold fruits and vegetables. The family had eight children, but her parents were determined that poverty would not decide their futures.Deshmane attended school in Kannada medium and would help her mother sell vegetables before and after classes. Her father, she recalled, had encouraged her to become a surgeon from a young age. When she entered medical college, however, the financial strain became even greater. Her mother reportedly sold her mangalsutra to help pay her daughter’s medical fees.The failure that almost made her give upHer path to becoming a doctor was not smooth. During medical school, Deshmane struggled with English and at one point failed physiology. She was so discouraged that she packed her bags and decided to return home.It was her younger sister who helped change her mind. Her sister reminded her that she too had experienced failure as a child but had not given up. Deshmane returned to college and eventually completed her MBBS from Karnataka Medical College in Hubballi. She went on to complete an MS in General Surgery from Government Medical College, Bellary, becoming the first woman to do so at the institution. She later trained in surgical oncology, including at Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai.“Give me surgery”For a woman entering surgery at the time, simply getting the opportunity was another battle. During her medical career, Deshmane recalled being questioned about what surgeries a woman could perform. At one point, she was offered gynaecology because it was considered more suitable for women.Her response was simple: “Give me surgery.” She eventually joined Kidwai Memorial Institute of Oncology in Bengaluru as a resident doctor. In 1994, she became the institute’s first woman professor. She later served as professor and head of the Department of Surgical Oncology and also as director-in-charge of the institute.Turning personal loss into a missionBreast cancer became a major focus of her work. She led global breast-cancer research projects and worked on improving surgical and treatment practices. Her connection to cancer was also deeply personal. Her mother and one of her sisters later died of cancer, experiences that strengthened her commitment to cancer awareness, early detection and research.Over roughly three decades at Kidwai, Deshmane also trained generations of doctors and worked to make cancer treatment more accessible. Her contributions included research into breast cancer and efforts to strengthen surgical-oncology education.Retirement was not the endDeshmane retired from surgical practice in 2015, but medicine and service remained central to her life. She continued working on cancer awareness and social initiatives and served as president of Abalashrama, an organisation supporting orphaned girls in Bengaluru. She also served in leadership roles connected with institutions including the National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research. In 2025, the Government of India honoured her with the Padma Shri for her contribution to oncology and breast-cancer research.The woman who once stood beside her mother selling vegetables eventually stood in an operating theatre as a surgeon, then in the corridors of one of Bengaluru’s leading cancer institutes as its first woman professor. Her story is not simply one of overcoming poverty. It is also a story about what can happen when a childhood shaped by sacrifice becomes the reason someone spends a lifetime making the road easier for others.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: In a scorching Spain, the traditional folding hand fan is having a moment
articles.summary: In crowded subway cars and sun-drenched plazas, an old-fashioned accessory in Spain has been everywhere thanks to the blistering summer heat.  Small enough t...
articles.body:
MADRID (AP) — In crowded subway cars and sun-drenched plazas, an old-fashioned accessory in Spain has been everywhere thanks to the blistering summer heat.

Small enough to fit into a purse, the traditional Spanish folding hand fan, or abanico, snaps open into a semicircle. With little more than a flick of the wrist, it creates a surprisingly strong breeze.

As successive heat waves in Western Europe pushed temperatures this summer to punishing levels, the accessory has become an essential, embraced by the young and old from Spain and elsewhere. Women — and a growing number of men — unfurl them on public transport, at concerts and at music festivals. In July, rainbow-colored abanicos were everywhere during Madrid's raucous Pride celebrations.

On a recent August day, 20-year-old Ana Feliu blocked the sun with a paper abanico she was gifted during a Valencian festival. She carries it everywhere in the summer, she said.

"This one is my favorite, but I have many," she told The Associated Press near Madrid's Puerta del Sol square. Temperatures in the Spanish capital are forecast to climb to 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit) on Thursday and Friday.

Also fanning himself was David González, whose abanico featured pinks, purples and reds.

"At first, I felt a little self-conscious, because it's something that's mainly associated with women, but I have to admit it serves a purpose — and it brightens my day," said González, 53.

Historians believe the folding fan reached Europe through Portuguese maritime trade with Asia in the 15th and 16th centuries.

As early as the mid-17th century, the Spanish painter Diego Velázquez made his enigmatic "The Lady with a Fan," in which a woman, possibly French, poses with what appears to be a delicate wooden abanico.

As they grew fashionable in European courts, Spain developed a taste and industry of its own. Madrid became an important center of production, and by the 18th century, Valencia had emerged as the Spanish fan-making capital.

So embedded was the abanico in Spanish aristocratic society by the 1800s that women used them to discreetly express flirtation, interest or disapproval through what was called "the language of the fan."

From Spain, the hand fan traveled to Latin America. In the 19th century, flamenco dancers began using the abanico as an expressive prop, as Cuban song and dance styles such as the guajira influenced the dance form. Over time, the fan's association with flamenco helped turn it into a quintessential Spanish symbol.

"The fan is a perfect element because, on the one hand, it evokes the heat and humidity of Cuba — that heavy, oppressive feeling," said Carmen Torres, a 44-year-old flamenco dancer in southern Spain. "And at the same time, it gives us a way to bring out the seductive, coquettish quality."

From century-old shops to souvenir kiosks

For more than a century and a half, Javier Llerandi's family has sold abanicos out of Casa de Diego, a wood-paneled shop in Madrid.

"We live from the heat," Llerandi told the AP.

The fans at Casa de Diego are made in Spain and range from simple two-tone wooden ones to elaborate, hand-painted items crafted from mother-of-pearl with intricate floral patterns. They start around 30 euros ($35), while others cost 200 to 500 euros (up to $580) and some high-end pieces reach 6,000 euros (nearly $7,000). Prices vary based on the materials used and, even more so, the workmanship involved, he said.

As Madrid has grown into a tourist hotspot, foreign visitors are also snatching up his fans, which Llerandi notes are more reliable than their portable, electric counterparts.

"Battery-run items eventually run out of power, and always at the worst possible moment," Llerandi said, adding with a smile: "Without a doubt, heat waves are good for this business."

And for the less discerning customer, plastic fans with printed designs are sold for a few euros at souvenir kiosks, including one a couple hundred meters from Llerandi's store. There, too, a salesperson reported strong sales this summer.

Outside a towering bullfighting ring in Madrid, Juani Duran sells wooden hand fans with traditional floral designs for five euros apiece at a stall. Bullfights take place in open-air stadiums, and spectators traditionally dress up to attend them, making the elegant fans a fitting accessory.

"You'll usually find a hand fan in any woman's pocket — and in some men's, too," Duran said before a late-August bullfight.

"They're not the best quality," she said, pointing at her stock, "but they'll get you through the summer."

AP photographer Laura León contributed from Seville, Spain.

articles.title: Algeria’s president seeks death penalty for those who start forest fires
articles.summary: Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s call comes after wildfires killed at least 12 people and injured 54 in northeastern Algeria.
articles.body:
Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune has called for the death penalty for anyone who deliberately starts a forest fire after at least 12 people died in wildfires in the country’s northeast.

Tebboune ordered Algeria’s justice minister on Sunday to submit a proposal by September 15 to amend the penal code to allow capital punishment for those convicted of intentionally setting forest fires, state media reported.

Algeria’s penal code already allows the death penalty for several offences, though the country has not carried one out since 1993.

Deliberately starting forest fires currently carries up to 30 years in prison, or life imprisonment in some cases.

Tebboune also ordered provincial governors to hand over all available information about the fires to security authorities, pointing to the possibility that some of the blazes were started deliberately.

“We saw videos and noticed that a number of fires broke out at the same time, at around 1am, which raises many questions,” he said.

His call came after Algeria observed three days of national mourning over the deaths of the 12 people in the provinces of Jijel, Bejaia, and Tizi Ouzou. At least 54 others were injured.

The president on Monday ordered authorities to compensate affected families and set up committees to assess losses and determine compensation for damaged property.

He instructed officials to restore electricity, gas, water and telecommunications in affected areas by Saturday at the latest, and told housing authorities to arrange repairs to damaged homes.

Tebboune said normal life should resume in the affected areas within a week.

At least 46 fires are still burning across the country, and a total of 193 fires have been recorded in the past 24 hours.

articles.title: Grand Canyon water pipeline damaged again as flooding complicates repairs
articles.summary: Flash flooding forced park closures and water restrictions at Grand Canyon as the $200 million pipeline repair project faces major new complications.
articles.body: The one pipeline that supplies water for millions of visitors in Grand Canyon was badly damaged by flash flooding over the weekend, setting up a complicated repair scenario and disrupting a yearslong project to upgrade the aging line across rugged terrain where helicopters are often needed for even basic maintenance. Park officials estimate after conducting flyovers that about 40% of the pipeline sustained damage. The 12.5-mile long Transcanyon Waterline has suffered dozens of breaks in recent years. A more than $200 million repair and replacement project was well underway when the floods began. The long-term impacts on the park’s infrastructure, visitors and year-round residents were not immediately clear. BELOVED TEXAS CHIROPRACTOR KILLED IN GRAND CANYON FLASH FLOOD, 2 FRIENDS STILL MISSING AFTER HIKE "We anticipate miles of the pipeline being destroyed," Grand Canyon Deputy Superintendent Brian Drapeaux said. A full survey of the devastation will not be completed until Tuesday at the earliest. At least two people died in the floods, and one person remained missing as of Monday night after roughly 80 people were rescued over the weekend, according to officials. The park stopped overnight accommodations, with officials saying significant water reductions are needed. This includes limiting shower time, turning off the tap while brushing teeth and flushing toilets selectively to protect the limited stored water on the South Rim, where most visitors frequent. "They have got to keep law enforcement going, they have to keep rescue operations going, backcountry operations, park admin going, the clinic and the campground," longtime river runner and Grand Canyon hiker Tom Martin said, adding that the park has hauled water in tanker trucks in the past. The pipeline, which was completed in the 1970s, has broken more than 85 times since 2010. The pipeline moves water from one side of the canyon, down to its base, across a bridge and back up the other side of the rough landscape. Any attempt to fix a break from rock falls or flash floods is precarious and costly and can take time, so fixing the latest damage will be complicated. The pipeline upgrade project, which began in 2023, took more than a decade to design and fund. The project involves installing helicopter pads, building water treatment facilities and replacing several miles of pipeline. It also seeks to move the water intake for the pipeline further down the canyon to Bright Angel Creek, which would put it closer to Phantom Ranch, a popular lodge at the base of the canyon. A 2018 evaluation of the project said key infrastructure for the intake would be outside of areas likely to flood. Officials said even basic decisions proved to be complicated. For example, the original pipe was aluminum, which is lighter and easier to move into the steep canyon but is more susceptible to breaking. Engineers chose a flex-steel material to balance weight and durability. Even routine pipeline breaks lead to water restrictions. A decade ago, a hotel on the canyon’s rim that offers luxury dining and highlights its history hosting presidents had to reduce dishwashing and use paper plates and plastic utensils. In 1995, a nearly month long repair on the pipeline required officials to truck in water. The park had water conservation initiatives in place even before the latest flooding and damage. MISSING GRAND CANYON HIKER, 83, RESCUED AFTER GETTING SEPARATED FROM COMPANION CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The flooding has forced parts of the park to close, and more flooding was possible on Monday, according to the National Park Service. "Consider changing your plans if you were going to hike, boat, or paddleboard to a slot canyon or normally dry wash. If you do still decide to recreate, check in at a nearby visitor center or ranger station," the park website reads. Officials previously said that the repair and replacement project would allow the park to meet its water supply needs for at least the next 50 years. As the original pipeline was nearing completion in the 1960s, more than a foot of rain fell, which flooded the inner canyon and caused 40% of the project to be destroyed, according to officials. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy’s future could rest with ‘prosecution doctors’ as case echoes infamous Maine killings: expert
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's murder jury ended a third day without a verdict as deliberations continue in the Massachusetts trial over her children's deaths.
articles.body: If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255). A retired Massachusetts Superior Court judge says that a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity wouldn't be an easy out for Lindsay Clancy, saying that "prosecution doctors" would be the ones deciding when she would be released, and are likely more inclined to keep her locked up. Clancy, 36, faces three counts of first-degree murder in the deaths of her children — Cora, Dawson and Callan, all under age 6 — who were found strangled at the family's home in January 2023. Retired Massachusetts Superior Judge Jack Lu told Fox News Digital that even if Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she would likely face a significant amount of time in a mental institution. ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY He said a group of mental health officials would be responsible for periodically reviewing her commitment at the facility, but noted these are people who overwhelmingly side with prosecutors and usually testify on their behalf. LINDSAY CLANCY PROSECUTORS COME ACROSS AS 'TONE DEAF,' 'UNCARING' AND 'SNARKY,' DEFENSE ATTORNEY SAYS "They're viewed as an arm of the prosecution," Lu said of the officials. "I'm going to be very frank, they kind of view this through the lens of if in doubt, lock them up...The people making release decisions have a prosecutorial mindset." SEND US A TIP Lu said, if Clancy is committed to a mental hospital, "I imagine she'd be committed year after year after year for some period of time." "If you are committed on a mental health basis because of a major criminal case in Massachusetts, it is hard to get out... It is very difficult," he said. He said there is another way for Clancy to be released from a mental institution if found not guilty by reason of insanity, which would be through the courts. "The other way she could get out is if the government kept moving to commit her and the doctors did not really decide that she should be released, and then it goes to court and then a judge would decide whether she is a danger to herself or others," Lu said. "It could be more of a contested hearing, and if she were to win that contested hearing, that is the second way that she gets out." LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE Clancy's case has drawn parallels with Constance Fisher, a then-24-year-old Maine woman who drowned her three children in a bathtub in 1954, according to the New York Times. LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST She was committed to a mental hospital, and after several years, she returned home. She was accused of drowning three more children in 1967 and was sent back to the mental hospital, before she escaped and was found dead in the Kennebec River. PROSECUTOR IN INFAMOUS KILLER MOM CASE SAYS WOMEN ON LINDSAY CLANCY JURY MAY BRING ‘STRANGE TWIST’ TO VERDICT The jury in Clancy's case, consisting of nine women and three men, led by a female foreperson, concluded a third day of deliberations on Monday without coming to a verdict. articles.title: CJP’s proposed march on Sep 5 an attempt to create lawlessness before Brics: PIL in SC
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to pass any interim orders on two PILs, including one by a retired police officer, seeking deferment of.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday refused to pass any interim orders on two PILs, including one by a retired police officer, seeking deferment of Cockroach Janata Party ‘s proposed march on Sep 5 by alleging that it is intended to create lawlessness ahead of Sep 12-13 BRICS summit in Delhi to deter participation of world leaders.When the petitioners questioned how such a march from the India Gate to the Police Headquarters can take place without permission, A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said there are two issues – one relates to law and order and the other to policy relating to permission to protest marches.“Let the stakeholders talk to them. As of now we have no reason to doubt that everyone would act and behave in a very responsible manner and in a peaceful and lawful manner. Right now, there is no compelling reason for us (the court) to presume that any wrong will happen. It is for the law enforcing agencies to ensure law and order while acting in accordance with law,” the CJI-led bench said.Appearing for one of the petitioners, advocate Syed Rizwan Ahmed said given the BRICS summit, till date no application seeking permission has been given to the authorities. In West Bengal, the previous govt did not give permission to so many protest rallies and the organizers had to move the HC for permission. Why does CJP, an unregistered entity not follow the same process? Are they above law, he asked.“God forbid another mishap, may not be by CJP, but by some mischievous elements take place, it will be covered by international media and deter participation of the foreign country leaders in BRICs,” he apprehended.The bench said, “All these factors are to be considered by some other quarters, not by us. There is nothing we can say right now. If something untoward or alarming happens, then file an application before us, provided the issue falls for determination in judicial domain.”The bench issued notice to the Centre on the two PILs, asked them to supply copies to the SC-constituted High-Powered Committee headed by retired SC judge R Subhash Reddy as well as the office of the solicitor general and posted these for hearing on Sep 10 along with petitions on July 20 incidents during protest march to Parliament, which turned violent resulting in alleged police excesses, injuries to protesters and security personnel and damage to public and private properties.When Ahmed asked whether CJP is above law and its processes, the bench said, “These are issues which are to be taken care of by the law and order enforcing agencies. It is their responsibility to maintain law and order. We expect both sides – protesters and law enforcing agencies - to respect, honour and follow the law of the land.”SC said it has referred a host of issues to the HPC, which is expected to give recommendations one after the other on them. When Ahmed persisted for a hearing on Sep 3 ahead of the proposed march, the bench said the petitioner must approach the Centre and Delhi police on the issue of absence of permission for the march. “Let them consider it,” it said.“There is no organized or identified group before us so that we can request them,” the bench said. Ahmed said that is another problem as CJP has no registered office where notice can be served. Can such an unorganized body hold the capital of the country to ransom, he asked.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: New storm names for 2026-2027 released by Met Office
articles.summary: Tuesday 1 September marks the start of the UK storm season and a new list of storm names have been released including Austen, Chloe and Evelyn.
articles.body:
The first of September marks the start of meteorological autumn, and with it the start of the UK's storm season.

In preparation for potential stormy spells, the Met Office has released a new list of names for the 2026-2027 season which have been chosen by members of the public.

This year, expect to hear the names Austen, Boelo and Chloe, which are the first three on the alphabetical list, followed by Dano and Evelyn.

Storms are named by the UK Met Office, Ireland's Met Éireann or the Netherlands' KNMI when they are forecast to cause "medium" or "high" impacts.

In the UK, storms are named when they are likely to cause disruption or damage that could lead to an amber or red warning being issued.

This decision is based on both the potential impact of the weather and how likely it is to occur.

Names are typically given to storms where impacts from strong winds are expected, although other weather-related effects are also taken into account such as heavy rainfall or snow which may lead to flooding or travel disruption.

Using one official system to name storms helps to share clear and consistent information about severe weather, making it easier for the public to stay safe.

The 2026-2027 marks the eleventh year of storm naming in the UK.

Storm names are selected jointly by the Met Office, Met Éireann and KNMI, with the final list aiming to reflect communities across the UK, Ireland and the Netherlands.

In 2025 the three meteorology agencies invited nominations for names from the public.

More than 40,000 were submitted - we saw names such as Amy, Isla and Marty selected for the 2025/2026 storm season.

This year's list continues to draw on those suggestions, reflecting not only popular choices, but also some of the personal stories behind them.

For example Austen was suggested in honour of Austen Nagle, the first director of the Irish Meteorological Service.

Chloe was selected by the Met Office after being nominated more than 130 times, including once by the mother of a five-year-old who is described by her mum as "fascinated by the weather" but can also "create a storm by herself" when she is tired.

And Ivy was nominated in honour of a nine-month-old Labrador puppy affectionately known as "the absolute destructor".

Any remnant of a tropical storm or hurricane that crosses the Atlantic will keep its original name, for example ex-Hurricane Erin, which brought a large swell to South West England in August 2025 and was named 'Storm Erin'.

To ensure consistency with the US National Hurricane Centre naming conventions, names that begin with the letters Q, U, X, Y and Z are not used.

Who decides when a storm should be named?

In Europe, there are five storm naming groups created from the meteorological agencies based in a similar geographic location.

The UK, Ireland, and the Netherlands form the western storm-naming group.

In the UK, storms are named when they are likely to cause disruption or damage that could lead to an amber or red warning.

Mostly this is because of strong winds but it could also be snow or heavy rainfall.

This decision is based on both the potential impact of the weather and how likely it is to happen.

However, it is worth noting that storms named by Met Éireann or KNMI due to forecast impacts in either Ireland or the Netherlands may not necessarily cause disruption here in the UK.

articles.title: 'I've never been to Afghanistan': Six million deportees forced to start over under the Taliban
articles.summary: As of August, the number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran had reached another million.
articles.body:
The elderly grimace, hobbling on crutches, and wide-eyed children stare, cradling chickens carried from homes they were forced to leave behind.

"It feels good to be in my own country," 35-year-old Nazia says, just minutes after she crosses from Pakistan, where she was born, into Afghanistan.

The Torkham crossing, known as "Zero Point", is where one hard life ends and another begins.

"But I've never been to Afghanistan before and many people here don't even have enough bread to eat," Nazia sighs as she heads, two of her children in tow, toward registration counters festooned with white and black Taliban flags.

Nearly her entire family, eight sisters and their offspring, were deported to Afghanistan this year from Pakistan or Iran.

They are part of the biggest cross-border movement of people anywhere in the world.

Millions of Afghans have fled across the borders to Pakistan and Iran for decades – seeking refuge or employment - and the number escaping Afghanistan has continued to rise since the Taliban takeover in August 2021.

Most are now being forced to return as these two neighbours crack down on undocumented migrants. Nazia and her family were undocumented but the UN and human rights groups say the security sweep is reaching far beyond that group to include registered Afghans too. Even Pakistan now publicly says that Afghans with Proof of Registration cards are not exempt.

The expulsions show no sign of stopping.

The number forced to return this year from Pakistan and Iran has already reached another million, according to the UN's Refugee Agency, the UNHCR.

"In a little under three years, we've seen six million people, a population that is itself the size of a small country, come back to Afghanistan," observes Charlie Goodlake, spokesperson for the UNHCR in Afghanistan.

"We've never seen in recent history a return movement on this scale," he underlines, standing in the baking heat in the tented village close to the border.

It's a desolate landscape of tarpaulin and plastic shelters, many now tattered and torn, erected by the UN and other aid agencies to provide refuge for a few nights for a people arriving with nowhere to go.

Many returnees have not set foot in Afghanistan for decades; many like Nazia have never been here at all.

"I left 45 years ago during the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and most of my brothers were born in Pakistan," explains Sarwar, who arrived a few days earlier with seven brothers and their families in a convoy of 40 people and the jumble of their worldly goods packed into a lumbering Pakistani lorry.

"We spent a long time there, so of course I felt heartbroken when they forced us out of our home," he says.

"But, despite all that pain, I am also happy because I am finally free of harassment by Pakistan's police."

Every family we met told us they had experienced prejudice and harassment by authorities in Pakistan.

The Pakistan government has not responded to the BBC's questions, but a foreign ministry spokesman told a briefing in Islamabad on Sunday that "the Government of Pakistan undertakes the necessary measures to prevent any instance of harassment or maltreatment of Afghan nationals in Pakistan. If such incidents have taken place, they are sporadic and are dealt with fully in accordance with the law".

Both Pakistan and Iran say it's past time for Afghans to go home, accusing some of posing a security risk, and others of being a financial burden.

The expulsions from Pakistan and alleged abuse intensified after a major escalation in fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan last October. In February, Human Rights Watch highlighted "door-to-door raids, late-night home searches and arrests without warrants".

In Iran, which claimed last year to host more than four million undocumented Afghans, the mass deportations were accelerated after its 12-day war with Israel and the US in June 2025.

The New York based Centre for Human Rights in Iran accused the authorities of using the post-war climate to "cast suspicion on Afghan migrants - accusing them of espionage and branding them as potential spies for Israel".

The UN's refugee agency continues to underscore the humanitarian principle that any return should be "voluntary, safe and dignified".

But in Torkham, Sarwar's sister-in-law Zarina laments the precarious future they face: "We have no resources to start a business or earn a living, and we don't even own a tent to live in".

Inside the barren transit tent, which provides little escape from scorching 41C heat, Zarina sits alongside an anxious huddle of women and their children.

Are they worried about the future for women and girls in a country where the Taliban has barred women from much of public life, including secondary school and university?

Forty-year-old Zarina turns to make a sweeping gesture with her arm: "Look at them, they're all girls. Of course I'm worried."

Some returnees are not just worried; they're terrified.

"I don't leave this house," a former Afghan security guard, first deported from Iran and then Pakistan, nervously tells us when we meet him far from the border in what he hopes is a safe house.

"We are all living in fear including my wife and children who are also afraid to go outside."

He dismisses the Taliban government's amnesty, announced days after their return to power which declared that former government officials, security personnel and civil servants would not face retaliation and were encouraged to return to work.

"I have no trust in their amnesty because many of my colleagues have been killed." He says his case had been registered with the UN but was deported before he could be transferred to a safer country.

Financial hardship magnifies the pain. The steep cuts in foreign aid worldwide are especially sharp in Afghanistan where the Taliban are still stuck in sanctions linked to terrorism and human rights.

Pakistan confirmed on Sunday that 16,000 vulnerable Afghans have now been granted, on humanitarian grounds, a temporary exemption from being deported – a decision welcomed by the UN.

But sources estimate that the number of Afghans in Pakistan at risk of serious harm, including women and girls who would be denied education, could be as high as 250,000.

At the graceful foreign ministry compound in Kabul, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi tries to put on a brave face.

"There's no doubt that we need some help," he admits. "There is pressure due to their return but in the long run, it will benefit them as well as Afghanistan."

In the first years after the Taliban swept to power in 2021, some of their ministers made light of humanitarian issues, saying God would provide.

The UN now estimates that 21.9 million people, nearly half the country, need assistance this year to survive. The UN's children agency, UNICEF, said last week that one million children faced "life-threatening" malnutrition.

"No country in the world could handle this kind of crisis on its own," UNHCR spokesperson Goodlake assesses, while acknowledging Taliban government efforts to help returnees as they arrive.

But, he adds, "We also know that many of the restrictions and edicts they put in place, particularly on women and girls, don't help us elicit international support".

Muttaqi reiterates his government's line that matters like girl's education are "internal issues" for Afghans to resolve.

The severe restrictions on the lives of girls and women is one of the major issues in the Taliban's international relationships and that has cost them. Five years on, only one country, Russia, has formally recognised their rule.

But when asked about this, Muttaqi points to the deepening diplomatic and economic ties with neighbours such as China and India, as well as Central Asian states.

As for Kabul's relative isolation from western nations, he asks, "those who didn't have relationships with us over the past five years, what have they achieved?"

We heard that word - "nothing" - from every family we met at Zero Point, but in a much different sense.

All were embarking on the hardest of homecomings, beginning all over again - with almost nothing.
