articles.title: Swinney says reform is at the heart of his programme for government
articles.summary: The first minister is due to set out his plans for the year ahead which are expected to include proposals for significant public service reform.
articles.body:
The first minister is due to set out his plans for the year ahead which are expected to include proposals for significant public service reform.

John Swinney said it was time to "embrace change", with reforms to sit at the heart of his programme for government.

He has already appointed a new cabinet minister to lead on public service reform and is also expected to set out a range of policies aimed at growing the economy, eradicating child poverty, transitioning to net zero and tackling violence against women and girls.

Opposition parties have said they want to see further action on the NHS and cost of living.

Swinney said he was committed to making sure Scotland delivered stronger economic growth, which he said would help tackle the challenges around child poverty and investment in public services.

And he said he would be setting out measures to parliament that would address "the epidemic of violence against women and girls".

Swinney is due to announce his programme for government to MSPs at the Scottish Parliament at 15:00.

He said: "The government came into office with a commitment to deliver a 100-day programme, and the government is going to do exactly that.

"And that's the first stage of me repaying the trust that the people of Scotland have put in my government, which is to deliver what I said to the public I would deliver."

He said the government had to review the way it delivered public services.

"We made clear before the election that was going to be necessary," he said.

"I want to make sure that the programme for government reflects the ambitions I set out in my election manifesto, which was all about making sure that we tackle the cost of living challenges that people face in Scotland, that we deliver improvements in our public services."

The first minister said the government "always lives within its means".

"Over the lifetime of the SNP government, we have balanced the budget on every occasion, and we will continue to do so," he said.

"But it also means that we've got to embrace change and change the way in which we deliver our public services."

He highlighted "significant improvements" in the NHS.

Swinney also said the government had made eradicating child poverty a priority and taken measures to make that possible through the delivery, for example, of the Scottish child payment and the expansion of whole family support.

"We work with families to help them out of poverty in addressing issues around housing or employability or, in some cases, addiction issues or childcare issues," he said.

"We're working alongside families to help those families get out of poverty and to make sure that children have the best chances of a start in life.

"It will be reinforced by the programme for government to make sure that the eradication of child poverty is written through all of the policy commitments of government to meet the expectations of the public in Scotland."

Business groups urge Swinney to scrap 'ineffective' food price cap plan

Swinney's 100-day push gives way to bigger battles ahead

We saw signs of domestic abuse, but we didn't know how to protect Stacy

The first minister said he had been "appalled" by the number of cases involving violence against women and girls over the summer months.

"This has been a long-running issue within Scottish society," he said.

"The government has taken many measures to tackle this, but I think events over the summer have said to me that I've got to exercise the strongest possible personal leadership as first minister to make sure that we tackle these issues."

He said violence against women and girls could not be tolerated "in any way, shape or form in our society" and added that "making sure that we change the behaviour of men and boys in our society will be central to that programme".

One of the government's proposals to tackle the cost of living issue was to introduce a price cap on some food and drink items in large supermarkets.

Twenty-three organisations have since written a joint letter to Swinney urging him to scrap the plan .

Signatories include groups representing retail, food and drink production, manufacturing and distribution businesses in Scotland.

In response, Swinney said: "Many members of the public are struggling with the price of their shopping and I want to try to do something practical to address that and that's about bringing forward a proposal for an affordable price cap on a limited number of items within our supermarkets.

"We've got to consult about this and make sure the legislation can have the effect that we want it to have and that's exactly what the government is going to do."

articles.title: Nottingham City Council underspend to help with cost of living
articles.summary: The council spent £20m less than expected last year.
articles.body:
Nottingham City Council is to provide more support with the cost of living after spending millions of pounds less than expected, the authority's deputy leader has said.

It was announced earlier this summer that the Labour-run council had underspent by more than £20m in the 2025-26 financial year.

Ethan Radford said details were still being finalised but the council would shortly announce a series of one-off measures "designed to alleviate pressure on individuals and businesses."

"Many of these policies will be things that we're piloting for one year, two years, to see what impact it has," he said.

"What it should be viewed as is a recovery package for parts of the city where it doesn't need year-on-year investment, but it needs an immediate injection of funding so it can get off the ground and have an immediate improvement."

He added that some of the money will also go towards fixing more potholes and further cleansing in the city centre.

"Getting rid of chewing gum, getting rid of grotty looking bins, getting rid of graffiti, the things that are unsightly that none of us want to see," he said.

It will not, however, be used to offset any potential future increase to council tax.

"At this time, we think it's better value for the taxpayer to take that £20m underspend and invest it into the services that they want to see improvement in," Radford said.

The council effectively declared itself bankrupt in 2023 but has recently shown signs of recovery.

Commissioners appointed to help run the authority in 2024 left earlier this year and were replaced with "ministerial envoys", who have fewer powers.

Radford said an underspend was "quite rare" but was evidence of the council's improving financial position.

Kirsty L Jones, leader of the Nottingham People's Alliance , however, said it may have come as a result of "under-delivery of services in the first place".

"I think when they've cut so deeply previously, it's not going to cause any sort of recovery in the services people expect, paying higher council tax for fewer services as they've seen throughout the years," she said.

"Helping with the cost of living - I don't know how they can meaningfully do that with £20m and expect to spend it on other things too."

The use of the underspend funds will be discussed at a meeting of the council's executive board on Tuesday.

It will then require approval from full council because it constitutes a change to the authority's annual budget.

articles.title: Scarborough B&B boss fears 'uneven playing field' tourist tax
articles.summary: The introduction of a tourism levy in North Yorkshire is currently under consideration.
articles.body:
A Scarborough bed and breakfast owner has said businesses like his will face an "uneven playing field" if a so-called tourist tax is introduced in North Yorkshire but not in neighbouring East Yorkshire.

A consultation on plans for a visitor levy closed in February and legislation is expected to be brought forward later this year.

James Rusden, who runs Scarborough's Toulson Court B&B, said if the levy was not England-wide, cost-of-living pressures would mean some visitors would instead go where no tourist tax was being charged.

A government spokesperson said: "We're listening to businesses in Yorkshire and across the country on this so we make sure money raised is invested in local priorities."

Rusden said he believed such a levy would act like "a form of taxation".

"Nobody likes an extra cost and people will complain about it," he said.

"But if it was an even playing field it would be a lot better as it would be easier to manage and control.

"People are short of money. To put a tax on them coming on holiday makes them think twice about where they go.

"If someone is coming to Scarborough but has to pay a levy each night, but can go to Bridlington where there's no levy, then that's where they'll go.

"It's unfair and it'll make it harder for us to compete."

Rusden said he was also concerned about the time the levy could be introduced, as people continued to struggle with the cost of living and faced further increases to energy bills.

A record season at Scarborough's Open Air Theatre, with its string of sold-out shows, had kept some North Bay B&Bs in business this year, Rusden said.

"We have a fantastic reputation and have won some good awards," he said.

"But we've discussed whether one of us has to go out and get a job to make up the difference and run the business differently.

"People used to come for four or five nights, they're now knocking a night off. They just can't afford it."

York and North Yorkshire's elected Labour mayor David Skaith said he believed a visitor levy "could be a total game-changer for us".

"York and North Yorkshire is beautiful, with something for everyone. Millions of people visit every year," he explained.

"Our visitor levy report was commissioned to understand the drawbacks and opportunities of the levy. We are taking time to review the feedback before we take our next steps."

However, Luke Campbell, Reform UK mayor for Hull and East Yorkshire, has previously said a levy would "not be the right approach" for his region.

Prof Brendan Paddison, Dean of York St John University's business school and chair of York Tourism Advisory Board, said research at the university has found a need to keep the tourism industry engaged in "decision-making and governance processes" around any proposed visitor levy.

"It also found a need that some of that funding that is perhaps raised through a levy is ring-fenced to support the industry and the work it does," Paddison said.

In Scarborough's North Bay, Phil and Carol Smith said they would still visit the resort even if a tourism levy was introduced.

Visiting from Derbyshire along with Logan the border terrier, Phil said he and Carol were married in Scarborough, stayed there at least three times a year and called the town their "second home".

Phil said he did not think a levy of £1 to £2 a night on an overnight stay would stop them making the trip.

"I'd rather not pay it, but that's nothing. A pint of Guinness is almost six quid, what's a pound? We feel comfortable here, everyone's so friendly."

However, both Phil and Carol questioned how and where the money would be invested, saying, for instance, that Scarborough needed more public toilets.

"It's a busy town. Some more places to sit, and especially some more public toilets, would be money well spent," Carol said.

Meanwhile, Charlie Highnett, who lives in East Yorkshire, said he would shop around accommodation providers for a cheaper deal in North Yorkshire in a bid to offset the cost of any levy.

"We really like coming to Scarborough, but it would be disappointing to pay any extra," he said.

"People want to come here and enjoy their holidays. I don't think any additional tax is needed, but if it is introduced it should be unified - not just one county."

He added that there should be "some alignment and joint decisions made".

Rod Fretwell, visiting Scarborough from his home in Bolton, said if the levy was being implemented nationally, he would support it.

"But if it singles out some businesses, like hotels and bed and breakfasts, and doesn't cover others, and it's not national - so you can go down the road and they don't charge it - then it shouldn't be done," he said.

Paddison said the findings of the consultation in North Yorkshire would provide "key industry insights" into the implications of any levy being introduced.

"There will also be learning from other countries and other areas in Europe that have a levy and the impact it's had - not just in terms of visitor numbers and the revenue generated, but how that money's spent," he said.

Skaith said: "We must get this right, because if we do, we can invest in what makes our county a fantastic place to live and visit like never before."

The government spokesperson said ministers were "delivering the biggest transfer of power, funding and responsibility from Westminster in a generation".

Mayors' new powers to introduce such a levy would mean local people benefited "even more" from tourism to their area, they said.

"When places grow their economies, they keep more of the rewards and can invest in what matters most to their communities."
